processing: As is usual for Uva estates, a black tea withered, rolled, fully oxidised and fired; the details of this estate's manufacture are little documented.
harvest_season: Picked through the year as on other Sri Lankan estates; Uva teas are generally most prized in the dry-weather quality season of the district.
appearance_dry: Typical of high-grown Ceylon: dark brown to near-black broken leaf.
appearance_liquor: Typical of the region: clear, bright reddish amber.
appearance_wet: Coppery brown broken leaf, as with other Uva black teas.
taste_profile: No detailed tasting record exists for this estate; expect what is typical of Uva black tea, brisk and bright with a clean, woody finish.

brewing.notes: Normally brewed Western-style, as with most Ceylon black tea. Milk is fine if the cup is strong enough to carry it.

vintage_note: Estate-specific sales are little documented. As usual for Ceylon black tea, it goes through the Colombo auction by grade and invoice and is best drunk within a year or two of manufacture; a seasonal date on the pack matters more than a year.
description:
Nayabedde is a tea estate on the slopes around Haputale in Uva. It is best thought of as a place name you may meet on a Ceylon invoice, rather than a famous tea with its own following.

The estate climbs a long way. A 1998 newspaper profile puts it at about 1,000 acres of tea, starting just above 4,000 feet and reaching 6,100 feet in its St Catherine's section, where its upper land meets Dambatenne and Pitaratmalie.

What the leaf tastes like from this garden in particular is little documented. Uva teas in general are brisk and bright, so that is the fair starting expectation, brewed Western-style with water just off the boil.

If you find it for sale, ask for the grade and the manufacture date. With a garden this tall, it is also worth asking which division the lot came from, though few sellers will know.
history:
Nayabedde's founding date and early owners are not clearly recorded. Its Visiting Agents' reports survive from 1920, which is unusual for plantation records, and the bungalow was rebuilt in stone and lime in 1925, replacing mud-brick walls. Ken Murray, a third-generation planter, was named in connection with its upkeep in 1998.

Today the Pekoe Trail walking route passes through St Catherine, a workers' village in its upper divisions.
